newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Vision says lower forecasts near mark.
newsitem.headline: Vision says lower forecasts near mark.

text.p: Vision Systems Ltd said on Tuesday analysts forecasts for a drop in net profit before abnormals in 1996/97 to about A$7 million were "not too far off the mark", but it expected significant improvements in earnings from new product launches in the next two years.

Vision managing director Jim Fox told a corporate briefing the final result for 1996/97 depended very much on the performance in the last couple of months of the year of the company's VESDA Laserplus smoke detector - the major reason for the reversal this year of the company's growth trend.

Vision Systems reported a A$10.6 million net profit in 1995/96, up from A$9.14 million the previous year, but has warned the market to expect lower earnings this year following delays in the launches of key products.

Fox told the Securities Institute of Australia briefing the company was hopeful it could secure a tender with the United States Navy for its upgraded laser airborne depth sounder (LADS) system, although he said a major threat could come through U.S. non-tariff trade barriers.
"As far as we know there is nothing out there that meets the specification but no contract is ever won till it is won and to be fair to the navy they may decide to change their requirement," he said.
Fox said he could not give any specific value to such a deal, but it would be worth "tens of millions of dollars" and would begin to have some impact, if it was won, in the 1997/98 year.

Vision's Smartwatch video security system, targetted at a market worth around A$500 million a year in the U.S., would not be in full production until August 1997 and if demand took off could be manufactured in Malaysia.

Smartwatch would make some contribution to the first half of 1997/98, but would really begin to "kick in" in the second half, with that year's earning potential being "anything from A$10-15 million", he said.
Fox said Vision System had had a tough year, most of which was self-inflicted but at least that meant it was reversible.
"It is positioned, I think, over the next two years to really capitalise on some of the pain we have taken this year," he said.
